items.title: 30.4.2 High-Resolution 1H NMR and Splitting of Peaks

source_refs.note: Topic 30.4.2 with Table 30.2 and Quick Check 30.3, answered (PDF 207-209); Figures 30.5 and 30.6 and the table's peak shapes are redrawn. Answers need review.

blocks.text: NMR signals are affected not only by nearby electrons but also by protons on the adjacent atoms. In a high-resolution spectrum each peak is often a cluster of sub-peaks, because the signal is split by the protons (1H) on adjacent carbon atoms. The splitting into multiple peaks (doublets, triplets, quartets) shows the number of protons on the neighbouring carbon atom. The number of sub-peaks follows the n + 1 rule: a signal usually splits into n + 1 sub-peaks, where n is the number of protons on the adjacent carbon atoms.

In the high-resolution spectrum of ethanol the -CH3 peak is split into three sub-peaks (a triplet), because the adjacent carbon has 2 protons (2 + 1 = 3), and the -CH2- peak into four sub-peaks (a quartet), because its adjacent carbon has 3 protons (3 + 1 = 4). The -OH signal is not split, because its hydrogen is bonded to oxygen rather than carbon. -OH and -NH protons usually do not show splitting and appear as singlets. Chemically equivalent protons do not split each other either: ethane, CH3-CH3, gives a single unsplit peak, because all its hydrogens are equivalent.

blocks.alt: Top: a sketch of the low-resolution 1H NMR spectrum of ethanol, three broad peaks at 5.4 ppm (1H, O-H), 3.7 ppm (2H, CH2) and 1.2 ppm (3H, CH3), with heights increasing in that order. Bottom: the high-resolution spectrum, a single line for O-H, four lines (quartet) for CH2 and three lines (triplet) for CH3.
blocks.caption: Low- and high-resolution 1H NMR spectra of ethanol (original sketches after Figures 30.4 and 30.5).
blocks.long_description: At low resolution each environment gives one peak, and the peak areas are in the ratio of the protons, 1:2:3. At high resolution the CH2 and CH3 peaks are split by each other's protons, while the O-H peak is not split.

blocks.alt: Four panels: a single line (singlet, no neighbouring protons); two equal lines (doublet, one neighbour, 1:1); three lines with the middle one twice as tall (triplet, two neighbours, 1:2:1); four lines with the middle two three times as tall as the outer ones (quartet, three neighbours, 1:3:3:1).
blocks.caption: Splitting patterns and the n + 1 rule (original diagram after Table 30.2).
blocks.long_description: A signal is split by the protons on the next carbon. One neighbour gives two lines, two neighbours three lines and three neighbours four lines, with the heights in the ratios shown.

blocks.alt: A high-resolution 1H NMR spectrum on a 3 to 0 ppm axis with a single unsplit peak near 0.9 ppm. Beside it, H3C-CH3 is labelled: all six hydrogen atoms are equivalent, so they do not split each other and the peak is a singlet.
blocks.caption: High-resolution 1H NMR spectrum of ethane: an unsplit singlet (original diagram after Figure 30.6).
blocks.long_description: Each methyl group of ethane has three protons on the next carbon, but those protons are equivalent to its own, and equivalent protons do not split each other. So even at high resolution ethane gives a single peak.

blocks.prompt: A signal in a 1H NMR spectrum is a quartet. How many adjacent, equivalent protons are there?
Give the number of sub-peaks for each signal of (i) butan-2-ol, (ii) 1-chloropropane, (iii) propanone, (iv) 2,2-dimethylpropane, (v) methanol.
blocks.explanation: (i) CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3: C1 CH3 doublet; C2 H six sub-peaks (5 neighbours); CH2 five sub-peaks (4 neighbours); C4 CH3 triplet; OH singlet. (ii) ClCH2CH2CH3: CH2Cl triplet; middle CH2 six sub-peaks (5 neighbours); CH3 triplet. (iii) Propanone: one singlet. (iv) 2,2-dimethylpropane: one singlet. (v) Methanol: CH3 singlet and OH singlet.

items: n + 1 rule: n protons on the adjacent carbon give n + 1 sub-peaks.
OH and NH usually singlets; equivalent protons do not split each other.
